name: golden-hammer
intent: Records what a Golden Hammer costs: one tool, platform or methodology applied to every problem because it is the one the team knows — and the price is a delivered solution that is measurably worse than a fit-appropriate alternative would have been, with the requirement quietly downgraded during scoping so nobody notices.
problem: A capability becomes the default answer before the problem is characterised. Competence bias, sunk training cost, organisational momentum and hiring constraints all point at the familiar tool, and the misfit cost of forcing it is invisible because it is deferred and easily attributed to the problem instead of the choice.
context: The name comes from Maslow's 'law of the instrument' and is catalogued in AntiPatterns. The DevIQ description is the most concrete: sometimes the Golden Hammer is the database, and logic that would be better off in the application ends up in the database because someone is more comfortable with SQL than with the application language; sometimes the reverse, and database-centric logic ends up in the application; other times the tool is the application platform, with an application built as a web or desktop app because that is where the developer feels comfortable rather than because it fits the client's needs. TechTarget attributes it to three conditions: solving so many problems with one tool that the team believes it addresses nearly any issue; sunk expenditure making alternatives unattractive; and 'it's always been that way' as the standing explanation for why a problem is never addressed. Its four warning signs are that the architecture is described in terms of one product or vendor suite, requirements go unmet because tooling does not meet project needs, no research into other approaches happens, and the whole lifecycle depends on one vendor or technology set.
benefits: It is a decision-time problem, not a build-time one, so it has a cheap remediation: profile the problem before choosing the tool, and run a spike against one alternative before committing.

The diagnosis is a re-attribution. A delivered solution that underperforms is normally blamed on the requirement; the Golden Hammer reading is that it is evidence the tool was chosen for fluency rather than for the problem's shape.

The boundary is parameterisable, so the accusation is not 'you reused too much'. Real investment in a stack — hiring, training, vendor ties, team identity — justifies some preference for the incumbent, and the line is drawn where misfit cost exceeds the saved acquisition cost.

It is cultural as much as technical, which means the interventions are organisational: case studies, proofs of concept, wider participation in tool selection, and tracking which dependencies the team has become dependent on.
tradeoffs: Tool familiarity has real value and the remedy cannot pretend otherwise. Acquisition cost of an alternative is front-loaded, visible and attributable; misfit cost is diffuse, deferred and easy to attribute elsewhere — that asymmetry, not stupidity, is the mechanism.

The interventions cost money. Case studies, proofs of concept, in-house learning groups and wider decision circles are unfunded work whose value is realised only if the team later chooses differently.

Polyglot is not free. Multiple technologies in production means multiple build pipelines, multiple deployment paths, multiple runbooks and more surface for incidents, and it can make the estate harder to operate than the monoculture it replaced.

Some expertise is a genuine asset. A team that is very good at one thing can deliver faster and more reliably in it than a team that is adequate at several, so spreading competence has an opportunity cost that the remedy ignores.

The signalling cost of choosing the incumbent is low and the signalling cost of choosing the alternative is high, which means the 'spike experiment' remedy is often skipped precisely when it is most needed.
Switching costs are real and asymmetric: the Golden Hammer critique applies most sharply to decisions still open, and is weakest where the decision has already been paid for.
quality_attributes_note: Scores describe the system while the smell is present. The striking feature is how flat this profile is, and that is the point: a Golden Hammer delivers a working system, which is why it survives. Coupling is the one axis that moves, because everything is bound to one platform's idioms, availability model and release cadence. Performance and scalability suffer indirectly and specifically — not because the tool is slow, but because it was never evaluated against the workload it was applied to.

participants.responsibility: The language, framework, database, platform or methodology applied to problems it was not selected for, chosen on fluency rather than fit.
participants.notes: It is not wrong; it is over-applied. The tool's real constraints were never measured against the problem's real requirements.

participants.responsibility: Carries fluency, training investment, hiring and identity in the incumbent, which sets the acquisition cost of any alternative above its actual cost.
participants.notes: DevIQ's four causes: competence bias, sunk cost, risk aversion towards the unknown, and organisational momentum.

participants.responsibility: The point at which the misfit cost is absorbed by quietly downgrading a requirement rather than by changing the tool.
participants.notes: This is the observable signature of the smell: a delivered solution measurably worse than a fit-appropriate alternative, plus a silently reduced requirement.

use_cases: SQL used for time-series or graph-shaped data because the team writes SQL well, with the traversal pushed into recursive CTEs and the alternative never evaluated.
A CRUD application written as microservices by a three-person team, because 'microservices are how you do DevOps'.
An event-streaming platform used for a nightly batch workload, adding operational burden with no latency requirement to justify it.
Always choosing the one language the team hires for, regardless of what the problem's shape demands.
XML used for everything because it was once the fashionable interchange format, including for formats better served by something else.
A relational ORM chosen for document data, with the schema fight becoming permanent engineering work.
avoid_when: The incumbent genuinely fits: the requirement matches what the tool was designed for, and the fit has been measured rather than assumed.

Switching costs are real and dominant — hiring pipeline, training already paid, vendor commitments, team identity — which is exactly the 'defensible reuse' region the parameter-based boundary describes.
The alternative's capability is worse on the dimensions that matter, and that comparison has actually been done.
Expertise concentration is a deliberate strategy for delivering faster in a narrow domain, with the concentration risk managed rather than ignored.
The decision has already been paid for and is not reversible at reasonable cost; the honest response is a planned exit with a date, not a rewrite.
You are choosing an open-source project over a proprietary one to reduce vendor lock-in, which is a genuine trade of one kind of dependency for another and should be made explicitly.
pitfalls: Treating the accusation as a ban on reuse. The failure mode is spreading into shallow competence across many tools with no depth anywhere.
Replacing familiarity with fashion. Choosing a new tool because it is current rather than because the problem fits is the same error with better branding.
Fixing it by adding a second stack permanently rather than by evaluating per problem. The goal is a decision process that can choose differently, not a polyglot estate.
Confusing familiarity with fit in the written ADR. 'The team knows it' is not a requirement, and a requirement list that omits it is the real evidence.
Ignoring the sunk-cost asymmetry in the team's own decisions: the same reasoning that justifies the incumbent should be applied to the alternative's acquisition cost.

related_patterns_notes.policy-based-design: Policy-based design is the structural answer to a subset of this: when one mechanism is applied where several are valid, the mechanism becomes a swappable policy and the choice becomes explicit rather than habitual.
related_patterns_notes.specification: Writing the requirements before the tool is the intervention that actually changes the outcome, because the requirement list is what the tool has to be measured against.
related_patterns_notes.strategy: Strategy is the code-level form of the remedy — isolating the part that varies so an alternative can be substituted — used where the Golden Hammer has been a single hard-coded choice.
related_patterns_notes.plugin: A plugin or extension point is what keeps a Golden Hammer from being a lifetime commitment: it bounds the area over which the choice is baked in.
related_patterns_notes.extension-object: An extension object lets a second tool be added without rewriting the first, which is the structural form of 'evaluate an alternative at decision time'.
related_patterns_notes.module: Modules give each area its own toolchain where the runtime permits it, which is how a Java or Python codebase can evaluate an alternative without rewriting the whole system.

anti_patterns: The 'we know it' rationale in an architecture decision record, with no requirement that the incumbent satisfies which another tool does not.
Requirements quietly downgraded during scoping so the tool's constraints fit — the observable signature that the tool, not the problem, set the shape.
An architecture described entirely in one product's vocabulary, with no line in the diagram that names a capability the product does not provide.
Requirements going unmet because the existing tooling does not meet the project's needs, while no alternative is ever evaluated.
No research into other approaches: no spikes, no case studies, no conference talks, no reading outside the incumbent's ecosystem.
Hiring constrained to one stack, so the next problem is also solved with the same hammer because there is no one who would use anything else.
Workarounds that fit the square peg to the round hole — subqueries in a relational database to emulate a graph, a stream processor to emulate a cron job.
The monoculture treated as an asset indefinitely, after the point where the switching cost it creates starts to dominate the fit it buys.
design_principles: Requirements before tools: a decision made against a written requirement list can be wrong in a way that is visible; a decision made against fluency cannot.
Make the misfit cost visible and front-loaded, because the asymmetry between a visible acquisition cost and a deferred misfit cost is the mechanism that produces the failure.
Preserve option value: prefer the structure that lets the choice be revisited — an interface, an extension point, a module boundary — over the one that bakes the tool in.
Choose for the problem's shape, not the tool's shape: a tool that requires the problem to be re-expressed in its idiom is a constraint, not a convenience.
Diversity of competence is resilience, and also a cost — both belong in the decision rather than one of them defaulting.
best_practices: Profile the problem before selecting the tool: throughput, latency, data shape, consistency needs, operating model. The requirement list is the instrument that changes the decision.
Run a time-boxed spike against one real alternative before committing, so the acquisition cost becomes front-loaded and the comparison is empirical rather than rhetorical.
Build a case study for the incumbent and for the alternative with the same dimensions — value provided, alternatives available, trade-offs — so the comparison is symmetric.
Expand who chooses: a decision made by three people is a decision made by their three biases. Wider input changes the candidate set before it is too late.
Track the dependency inventory explicitly — which tool the whole lifecycle depends on, and which are one team's competence away from being unusable.
Set evaluation triggers in advance: a load threshold, a support end-of-life, a hiring change, a requirement that the current tool cannot meet.
Practise the 'extra five minutes' discipline: before choosing the familiar tool for an unfamiliar problem, spend a bounded amount of time checking whether the intended solution is viable at all.
Where the incumbent is retained deliberately, record it as accepted lock-in with a rationale and a review date, so it is a decision rather than an unexamined default.
sources: DevIQ antipattern catalogue, 'Golden Hammer' — the database logic example in both directions, the platform example, and the Shiny Toy relationship.

Twain Taylor, 'Signs of a Golden Hammer antipattern, and 5 ways to avoid it', TechTarget, 2022 — the three root conditions (success breeds overconfidence; sunk spend; 'it's always been that way'), the four warning signs, and the five practices including case studies, in-house learning groups and wider decision circles.

Kurt Zoglmann, 'Golden Hammer Anti-Pattern', The Encyclopedia of Abstractions — the structural mechanism of asymmetric cost salience, the parameter-located boundary between defensible reuse and pathological inertia, and the remediation set (problem profiling, spike experiments, option-value preservation, tool-inventory audits, post-mortems).
Abraham Maslow, 'The Psychology of Science' (1966) — the law of the instrument, the proverb's origin.
William H. Brown, John W. Rozdial, Will P. Yost, 'AntiPatterns: Reengineering Software Architectures', Addison-Wesley, 1998 — the catalogued source of the name.
